column1: At 48kHz with a 128-sample buffer, how much time does processBlock() have before the host needs the next block?
column2: 2.67 ms (128/48000). Missing this deadline causes an audible click, pop, or dropout — there is no buffering your way out of it after the fact.

column1: What are the four operations strictly forbidden inside the audio callback thread (processBlock)?
column2: No memory allocation (malloc/new), no mutex locks, no file/network I/O, and no logging (e.g., std::cout or DBG). Any of these can block unpredictably and cause a missed deadline.

column1: How do the UI thread, audio thread, and message thread communicate in a real-time safe plugin?
column2: Exclusively through lock-free mechanisms: atomics for single values (e.g., cutoff frequency) and lock-free FIFOs for streams (e.g., MIDI events, meter data). They never share a mutex.

column1: What causes 'zipper noise' and how is it fixed?
column2: Reading a smoothed parameter value once per block and holding it constant across all samples causes audible stepping during fast automation. Fix: per-sample parameter interpolation (e.g., juce::SmoothedValue or a hand-rolled ramp), not a coarser UI.

column1: What are denormal numbers and why do they cause audio glitches?
column2: Denormals are floating-point values in the range ~1e-38 to 1e-308 that occur as feedback loops (reverb tails, filter resonance) decay toward zero. x86 CPUs process them 10–100× slower in hardware, causing real-time glitches ('crackling silence'). Fixed via DC bias, flush-to-zero checks, or FTZ/DAZ CPU flags.

column1: Why must filter cutoff and resonance/Q be clamped in code rather than relying on GUI slider ranges?
column2: Any IIR/feedback filter has a pole in the Z-plane; if its magnitude reaches or exceeds 1.0 (e.g., cutoff briefly exceeding Nyquist during a fast sweep, or resonance maxed out), the filter blows up to infinity or NaN within milliseconds. Clamp cutoff to [20 Hz, 0.49 × sampleRate] and clamp resonance to a tested max in code.

column1: What is the causality invariant for DSP code, and when is an exception allowed?
column2: Output at sample n can only use input from samples ≤ n. The only exception is a look-ahead process (e.g., a limiter) that deliberately buffers future samples AND reports the resulting latency to the host.

column1: Why do distortion/saturation plugins oversample 2x–8x internally?
column2: Nonlinear processes (saturation, hard clipping, waveshaping) generate harmonics that can exceed the Nyquist frequency. Oversampling moves the folding point up, allowing filtering before downsampling back, preventing aliasing (wrong, inharmonic pitches).

column1: In a band-limited synth voice architecture, why must oscillators be band-limited at the source (e.g., PolyBLEP) rather than filtered afterward?
column2: Aliased energy folds into the audible spectrum and cannot be separated from real harmonics once it exists — filtering after the fact cannot remove it, so band-limiting must happen at generation time.

column1: Give a concrete aliasing example: a naive sawtooth at C7 (2093 Hz) played at 48kHz — what happens to harmonic 12?
column2: Harmonic 12 = 12 × 2093 = 25,116 Hz, which exceeds Nyquist (24,000 Hz). It folds back to 48,000 − 25,116 = 22,884 Hz at about −21.6 dB relative to the fundamental — audible, and it moves down in pitch as the played note moves up.

column1: Why is renaming a parameter ID in a shipped plugin dangerous?
column2: Plugin state is the parameter tree and nothing else; parameter IDs are permanent identifiers used in saved project files. Renaming one silently breaks every saved project that referenced it.

column1: How must MIDI events be handled within an audio buffer to be 'sample-accurate', and what is the common mistake?
column2: The host buffer must be split at each MIDI event's sample offset (e.g., via juce::Synthesiser) so notes trigger at their exact sample position. The common mistake is applying all MIDI events at the start of the block, which smears timing.
